question:
Read the following passage and answer the question.

Employers routinely pay more for job candidates holding a university degree than for those without one, even when the degree's subject bears no relation to the job's actual duties. The conventional explanation treats education as a factory that manufactures skill: years in a classroom build competence, and wages simply reward that competence. But a rival account treats the degree not as proof of what was learned but as evidence of what the holder was already capable of enduring. On this view, a demanding and lengthy course of study functions less as a training ground than as a filter: it is costly enough that only the more able, disciplined, or persistent candidates find it worth completing, and it is this pre-existing quality, not any skill imparted by the coursework, that employers are actually paying for.

The two accounts are not easy to tell apart from the outside, since both predict the same correlation between credentials and wages. But they diverge sharply in their implications. If education is a factory, its value lies in the material taught, and shortening or cheapening the process would erode the very competence employers seek. If education is a filter, its value lies in the cost of passing through it: the arduousness must remain high enough to separate the able from the merely willing, whatever the syllabus actually contains. A short, easy, universally-awarded credential would signal nothing at all, however accurately it reflected some minimal literacy.

This second account unsettles the usual case for expanding access to credentials. If a qualification's worth to the labour market rests substantially on its scarcity and difficulty, then making it easier to obtain, however admirable on grounds of fairness, may erode the very information employers rely on to distinguish candidates, forcing them to search for some costlier signal in its place. The problem, then, is not that credentials fail to inform employers, but that the information they carry may have little to do with the classroom at all.

Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: (a) Education always increases a worker's productive skill.
(b) Employers pay more for degree-holders because degrees may signal pre-existing ability rather than impart it.
(c) Universities should be shut down because they teach nothing of value.
(d) Wages are determined solely by the difficulty of a course of study.
explanation: The passage's central move is contrasting the 'factory' (skill-building) account with the 'filter' (signaling) account, and arguing employers may be paying for the signal, not the skill.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Reading Comprehension — main idea (economic/signaling theory passage)

The claim that 'a short, easy, universally-awarded credential would signal nothing at all' rests most directly on which assumption?

(b) All credentials are equally difficult to obtain.
(c) Employers can never observe a worker's actual output.
(d) Skill and ability are identical concepts.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question.

We are accustomed to defending privacy as a shield: a boundary that keeps unwanted eyes from matters we would rather keep to ourselves, useful chiefly to those with something to hide. On this account, the person with nothing embarrassing in their life loses little by being transparent, and privacy is simply a convenience that shrinks as our conduct grows more blameless. Yet this treats privacy as though its only function were concealment, and misses a subtler role it plays in the very formation of a self.

To be watched is not merely to be seen; it is to perform. The presence of an observer, even an imagined one, alters what a person does, tempering experiment with the awareness that missteps will be recorded and judged. A self that is never unobserved has little room to try on a belief before endorsing it, to rehearse a version of itself that might be abandoned without cost, or to fail privately before succeeding publicly. Privacy, on this reading, is not the opposite of a full life but one of its preconditions: the unwatched interval in which a person drafts themselves before committing to a final version for others to see.

This suggests that the harm of pervasive surveillance is not exhausted by the risk that some secret will be exposed. Even a population that is never actually punished for what is observed may still be subtly altered by the mere fact of being watched, converging toward whatever is safest to display and abandoning the tentative, the experimental, the not-yet-decided. A society that dissolves privacy in the name of having nothing to hide may thereby lose something it did not know it possessed: the private draft from which a considered self is written, long before it is fit to be shown.

Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) Privacy matters only to people who have something to hide.
(b) Being watched, even without punishment, can narrow a person's room to experiment and form a self, so privacy is a precondition of that formation, not merely concealment.
(c) Surveillance should be banned because it always leads to punishment.
(d) A fully transparent society is always a freer society.
explanation: The passage argues privacy is not just concealment but a precondition for a self to form via unwatched experimentation.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Reading Comprehension — main idea (privacy and the self passage)

question:
Five friends — P, Q, R, S and T — sit in a row, each facing either north or south.
(i) P sits third from the left end.
(ii) Only one person sits between P and Q, and Q sits to the left of P.
(iii) T sits immediately to the right of P.
(iv) R sits second to the right of P.
(v) Exactly two people in the row face south, and S is one of them.
(vi) Q faces north.
(vii) T and R face the same direction as each other, and this direction is different from P's direction.

Who sits at the left end and the right end of the row respectively, and which direction does each face?
explanation: Positions (left to right): P=3rd from left. Q is left of P with exactly one person between → Q=1. T is immediately right of P → T=4. R is second to the right of P → R=5. The remaining seat, position 2, goes to S. For facing: Q faces North (given). Exactly two face South, one being S; T and R face the same direction, opposite to P. If P=South, T=R=North, giving South-facers = {S,P} = exactly 2 (consistent). If P=North, T=R=South, giving three South-facers (contradiction). So P=South, T=North, R=North. Left end = Q (North), right end = R (North).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Linear seating arrangement with facing directions

question:
Four colleagues — J, K, L and M — each live in a different city (Delhi, Pune, Kochi, Patna) and each has a different profession (Doctor, Engineer, Teacher, Lawyer).
1. J is not from Delhi or Pune.
2. The Engineer is from Kochi.
3. K is a Doctor and is from Patna.
4. L is not an Engineer.
5. M is from Delhi.
6. M is not a Lawyer.

Who is the Lawyer, and which city is this person from?
explanation: K=Doctor/Patna (clue 3). M=Delhi (clue 5). J is not Delhi/Pune (clue 1), and Patna is taken, so J=Kochi. The only city left, Pune, goes to L. The Engineer is from Kochi (clue 2) = J, so J=Engineer. Remaining professions Teacher/Lawyer go to M and L; M is not a Lawyer (clue 6), so M=Teacher and L=Lawyer, from Pune.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Matching puzzle — city and profession

question:
In each question below, statements are followed by conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All doctors are engineers. Some engineers are teachers. No teacher is a painter.

Conclusions:
I. Some doctors are teachers.
II. No engineer is a painter.
III. Some teachers are engineers.
explanation: "Some engineers are teachers" converts validly to "Some teachers are engineers" (a particular affirmative always converts) — so III always follows. I does not follow: the doctors (subset of engineers) need not overlap with the specific engineers who are teachers. II does not follow: only the teacher-subset of engineers is known to be disjoint from painters; other engineers could still be painters. Hence only III follows.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Categorical syllogism

question: In a certain code language, TEACHER is written as VGCEJGT. How is CHILDREN written in that code?
explanation: The code shifts every letter forward by 2 positions in the alphabet (T→V, E→G, A→C, C→E, H→J, E→G, R→T, all confirmed +2). Applying the same shift to CHILDREN: C→E, H→J, I→K, L→N, D→F, R→T, E→G, N→P, giving EJKNFTGP.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Coding-decoding — alphabet shift cipher

question: Pointing to a man, Reena said, "He is the son of the only son of my father." How is the man related to Reena?
explanation: "The only son of my father" is Reena's brother (her father has exactly one son, and Reena is his sibling). "He is the son of [that brother]" makes the man the brother's son — i.e., Reena's nephew.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Blood relations riddle

question: A man walks 8 km towards North. He then turns right and walks 6 km. He then turns right again and walks 8 km. He then turns left and walks 4 km. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
explanation: Taking start at (0,0) facing North: walk 8 km North → (0,8). Turn right (North→East), walk 6 km → (6,8). Turn right again (East→South), walk 8 km → (6,0). Turn left (South→East), walk 4 km → (10,0). Straight-line distance from (0,0) to (10,0) = 10 km, due East.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Direction and distance

question:
The table below shows the number of students enrolled in five courses at a college, for 2024 and 2025.

Course | 2024 | 2025
P | 240 | 300
Q | 180 | 150
R | 320 | 400
S | 150 | 210
T | 210 | 240

What is the percentage increase in enrollment in Course S from 2024 to 2025?
explanation: Course S: (210−150)/150 × 100 = 60/150 × 100 = 40%. Option (d) 60% is a trap — it uses the raw absolute increase as if it were the percentage.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Percentage change from a data table

question: You are a newly posted Sub-Divisional Magistrate. On a village visit, you find the local school has not received mid-day meal supplies for two weeks due to a contractor dispute, and children are going hungry. The contractor blames the previous SDM for unpaid dues; the current supplier refuses to continue without payment; parents are angry and threaten to stop sending children to school. What should you do?
options: (a) Ignore the issue since it predates your posting and is a financial matter for the previous administration.

(b) Arrange an emergency stop-gap supply of food through local resources or discretionary funds immediately, while simultaneously initiating a formal inquiry into the pending dues and a resolution with the contractor.
(c) Publicly reprimand the contractor in front of the parents to pacify their anger, and defer any resolution of payment until headquarters responds.
(d) Advise the parents to arrange food for their children privately until the dispute is resolved through the courts.
explanation: Balances the immediate humanitarian need (children must eat now) with due process on the underlying financial dispute; doesn't pass the buck, grandstand, or leave the resolution to courts/parents alone.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Administrative crisis response — balancing urgency and due process

question: Two of your team members, X and Y, are both competent but have a personal rivalry that is beginning to affect team output. X refuses to share critical data with Y, citing "security concerns," though you suspect this is really about the rivalry. A project deadline is approaching. What is the best course of action?
options: (a) Take X's stated reason at face value and formally restrict Y's access, avoiding the interpersonal issue entirely.

(b) Speak privately with both X and Y to understand the root of the conflict, clarify the data-sharing protocols the project actually requires, and set clear expectations for cooperation, escalating only if the behaviour continues.
(c) Publicly criticize X in a team meeting for withholding data, to pressure a change in behaviour.
(d) Reassign all of Y's work to another team member to avoid dealing with X, and let the deadline slip if necessary.
explanation: Addresses the real interpersonal root cause privately and professionally, sets clear expectations, and reserves escalation for continued non-compliance — firm but not punitive or avoidant.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Interpersonal conflict management in a team

question: As the officer in charge of a relief camp after a flood, you notice a local NGO distributing extra blankets and food only to families of a particular community, while some equally needy families from other communities go without. When you raise this with the NGO coordinator, they say it is because those families "reached out first." What should you do?
options: (a) Allow the NGO to continue as is, since they are volunteers and their assistance is voluntary and unpaid.
(b) Immediately expel the NGO from the camp without further discussion, since discrimination has occurred.

(c) Direct that all relief distribution in the camp be conducted through a transparent, needs-based register maintained by camp authorities, ensure the NGO's contribution is pooled into the common resource for equitable distribution, and monitor for compliance.
(d) Ask the affected families to file a formal complaint before taking any action.
explanation: Restores fairness through a transparent, needs-based system under camp authority rather than either tolerating discrimination, overreacting by expelling a well-meaning NGO outright, or placing the burden of complaint on already-vulnerable families.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Equitable disaster relief distribution

question: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours, and Pipe B can fill it in 16 hours. Both pipes are opened together, but after 4 hours, Pipe A is shut off. In how many more hours will Pipe B alone fill the remaining tank?
explanation: Combined rate for 4 hours: 4×(1/12+1/16) = 4×(4/48+3/48) = 4×7/48 = 28/48 = 7/12 of the tank filled. Remaining = 1 − 7/12 = 5/12. Pipe B alone: time = (5/12) ÷ (1/16) = 5/12 × 16 = 80/12 = 20/3 hours = 6 hours 40 minutes.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Pipes and cisterns — partial work and remaining rate

question: A vessel contains a mixture of milk and water in the ratio 5:3. When 16 litres of the mixture is removed and replaced with pure water, the new ratio of milk to water becomes 5:7. Find the initial quantity of the mixture in the vessel.
explanation: Let initial volume = V. Milk = 5V/8, water = 3V/8. Removing 16 L of mixture removes milk and water in the same 5:3 ratio: milk removed = 16×5/8 = 10, water removed = 16×3/8 = 6. After removal and adding 16 L pure water: milk = 5V/8 − 10, water = 3V/8 + 10. New ratio: (5V/8 − 10)/(3V/8 + 10) = 5/7. Cross-multiplying: 7(5V/8 − 10) = 5(3V/8 + 10) → 35V/8 − 70 = 15V/8 + 50 → 20V/8 = 120 → V = 48. Check: milk=30, water=18; remove 16 L → milk=20, water=12; add 16 L water → water=28; ratio 20:28 = 5:7 ✓.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Mixtures and alligation — replacement problems
